issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot obtain statutory restoration of possession on the basis of a compromise breach alone, and a qualifying prior termination of the tenancy cannot be inferred without support in the record.
material_facts: The landholder had leased the lands to the tenants and later obtained possession under a compromise that required personal cultivation and restricted leasing to others if he did not cultivate personally.
The landholder later placed the lands in the possession of other persons under agreements to sell them.

The tenants sought possession, stating that the landholder had breached the compromise; their application did not plead termination under the statutory provision for resumption for personal cultivation or a claim under the related restoration provisions.
The landholder's original application for possession was not in the record, so its ground for seeking possession could not be determined.

The High Court treated the tenants' application as one under the statutory restoration provision and inferred that the landholder had terminated the tenancy for personal cultivation, without a basis for that finding in the available material.
It was accepted, and not challenged before the Supreme Court, that the tenants' application would be time-barred if it were an application under the provision they had invoked.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the landholder had acted under the personal-cultivation termination provision was unsupported on the available record. A breach of the compromise alone did not entitle the tenants to rely on the statutory restoration provision. The High Court's order was set aside and the matter remitted to the Revenue Tribunal, which could obtain the landholder's original application and determine the true nature of those proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 44 and 45 of the Hyderabad Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1950, the statutory restoration remedy described by the Court depended on a tenancy having been terminated on the specified ground of personal cultivation, followed by failure to cultivate as required. Section 46 could not assist tenants where the only established matter was breach of a compromise; the nature of the landholder's proceedings had to be determined from the material, including the original possession application. No earlier cases were relied on. The limitation conclusion concerning an application under Section 32 was not challenged and was not the issue decided.

predicates.tenant_possession_proceeding: Tenants brought a proceeding seeking possession of land from a landholder.
predicates.compromise_breach_was_only_stated_ground: The tenants relied on the landholder's breach of a compromise as the stated ground for seeking possession.
predicates.original_landholder_application_was_unav: The landholder's original application for possession was not available in the record being reviewed.
predicates.qualifying_termination_was_inferred_with: The reviewing court inferred a qualifying termination of the tenancy without supporting material in the available record.

issues.definition: When tenants seek possession based on a compromise breach and the underlying application is unavailable, an unsupported inference of a qualifying termination requires the finding to be set aside and the matter remitted.
